title: Area I review: Fundamentals of Instructing
intro: These questions mix all six Tasks of Area I: human behavior and communication, the learning process, lesson planning and classroom methods, assessment, professional responsibilities, and risk management. Many join two of them in one real teaching situation, the way an examiner would ask.

questions.q: Your learner's landings improved fast for six lessons, but for the last three they have not gotten any better, and her stage check is two weeks away. You have flown nothing but pattern work to get her ready. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Keep flying only pattern work until the landings improve, since the stage check is close
Treat the plateau as a sign that learning has stopped and postpone the stage check until she shows new progress
Arrange an evaluation flight with an instructor who does not know her, since a plateau suggests a psychological problem
Tell her plateaus are normal and temporary, give landings a break by moving to another part of the syllabus, and consider that your own over-practice may have caused it
questions.why: After fast early gains, a plateau is normal in motor skills and does not mean learning has stopped. Explain that it is normal and temporary, move the learner to a different place in the curriculum to give the task a break, and remember that the instructor can bring on a plateau by over-practice [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. Plateaus are a common source of frustration and lower motivation, so assure her that improvement will resume with effort [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. More of the same pattern drill is the over-practice that may be causing it, and the unbiased evaluation flight is for a suspected serious psychological problem, not a normal plateau [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

questions.q: On her first steep turns your learner locks her eyes on the altimeter, misses the traffic you point out and grips the yoke hard. Afterward she admits she was scared the whole time. Which response best fits what the AIH teaches?
options: Warn her that her stage check will go badly if she cannot relax, to raise her effort
Fly steep turns again right away and keep repeating them until the fear is gone
Recognize that fear narrowed her perception, treat it as a normal reaction, and ease her back into steep turns with a clear description of what she will see and feel
Drop steep turns from the flight lessons and cover them only on the ground
questions.why: Fear narrows the perceptual field, and the AIH's own example is a learner staring at the altimeter in her first steep turns. Threats of unsatisfactory reports do not work psychologically, and if a situation seems overwhelming to the learner, a threat exists [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]. Treat fears as a normal reaction and introduce anxiety-causing maneuvers with care so the learner knows what to expect [[25:45|AIH 2-12]], easing her into the feared flight region carefully [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. The stage check warning is the threat the AIH rejects, and dropping the maneuver leaves a required skill untrained.

questions.q: A motivated learner meets the slow flight goal on her first two tries, but the syllabus gives slow flight three full lessons, so you keep drilling it. By the second lesson she is bored and getting sloppy. What does the AIH say is going on?
options: Instruction paced for a slower learner is breeding impatience and disinterest; move her to the next step as soon as each goal is met
She has reached the automatic response stage and should never practice slow flight again
She is using the defense mechanism of compensation by finding fault with the syllabus
Slow flight must be repeated a fixed number of times before any new task can start
questions.why: Impatience can come from instruction keyed to the pace of a slow learner when it is applied to a motivated, fast learner. Advancing a learner as soon as one goal is met matters as much as finishing each step, and disinterest grows rapidly with unnecessary drill on what is already learned [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. The instructor can also bring on a plateau by over-practice [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. Compensation is covering a weakness by stressing a strength in another area [[25:43|AIH 2-10]], which is not what she is doing, and nothing in the AIH sets a fixed repetition count.

questions.q: Briefing a landing lesson, you tell your learner, "If the approach falls apart, take appropriate measures." On short final the approach goes badly and she just keeps descending. What communication problem does the AIH point to, and what should you have said?
options: Interference from cabin noise; you should have repeated the same words louder
Overuse of an abstraction; a concrete instruction such as "go around" means the same action to both of you
Confusion between the symbol and the object; you should have avoided the word "approach"
Lack of common experience; she needs many more landings before any briefing can work
questions.why: Abstract words do not call up the same specific picture in each mind. The AIH uses this exact case: telling a learner to take appropriate measures when an approach is going badly may not produce the desired action, while telling her to go around has the same meaning to both of you [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. The same advice runs through lecture planning: specific words tell more than general ones [[25:115|AIH 5-12]]. Saying the vague phrase louder does not make it concrete, and the problem was the general wording, not the word approach.

questions.q: Your adult learner wants to fly his family to a lake cabin next summer, and he calls weight and balance boring. Which opening for today's ground lesson on it best fits both the AIH lesson introduction and its advice on tangible rewards?
options: A joke about pilots and coffee to relax him before the numbers start
A list of accidents caused by overloading, so fear keeps him paying attention
A quick statement of the formulas, then straight into the development
A question about what his family and their bags weigh, why today's lesson decides whether that load can safely and legally make the lake trip, then a short road map of the lesson
questions.why: A lesson introduction has three elements: attention, motivation and an overview. The attention step should relate to the subject, since an unrelated joke distracts, and the motivation step gives specific reasons the content matters that appeal to each learner personally, which ensures readiness [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]. The tangible rewards of a lesson are not always obvious, so relate its objective to an operational need the learner cares about [[25:36|AIH 2-3]]. A fear-based opening is negative motivation, which is not as effective as positive motivation [[25:35|AIH 2-2]], and jumping to the formulas skips attention and motivation.

questions.q: Your learner is copying the taxi clearance from ground control when you start explaining how you want the first maneuver of the lesson flown. She reads back the wrong taxiway. What does the AIH say explains this?
options: Coding information into short-term memory takes 5 to 10 seconds and is easily lost if interrupted, and adding a second task cuts comprehension and recall of both
Short-term memory holds information for about 30 minutes, and your newer explanation replaced the clearance
Long-term memory is a perfect recording, so she has now stored the wrong taxiway permanently
Repression: she pushed the clearance out of reach to avoid an unpleasant feeling
questions.why: Short-term memory holds information for roughly 30 seconds; coding takes 5 to 10 seconds, and if coding is interrupted the information is easily lost [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. The AIH adds that a higher-level task needs concentration and that adding even a simple activity diminishes comprehension and recall of both [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. Short-term memory works in seconds, not minutes; long-term memory is a reconstruction, not a perfect recording [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]; and repression is an unconscious way of forgetting unpleasant memories [[25:89|AIH 3-38]], not a busy moment on the ramp.

questions.q: Your learner's turn entries are smooth whenever you ask for one in the practice area, but in the traffic pattern she skids the turn to final and forgets to clear before turning crosswind. Which level of learning has she not yet reached for turn entries?
options: Rote
Understanding
Application
Correlation
questions.why: Consistent turn entries after demonstration and practice mark the application level, and the AIH warns that instructors too often stop there, which is piecemeal instruction. Correlation, which should be the objective of aviation instruction, is the ability to tie turn entries to other blocks of learning, and the AIH's example is using them correctly in traffic patterns [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. She is past rote and understanding because she already flies good entries on their own; what is missing is carrying them into the pattern.

questions.q: The lesson before a stage check, your learner flies twelve short-field landings in a row and the last four are excellent. At the start of the next lesson her first short-field landing is well outside standards. What does the AIH say about this?
options: Repeating one task over and over improves performance during the session but gives poorer long-term learning and can fool learner and instructor alike; mixing tasks, as in a scenario, gives better retention
Her skill reached the automatic response stage during the twelve landings and only needs a warm-up
Random practice caused it; she should have flown only short-field landings that day
It proves she is on a learning plateau, so short-field landings should be dropped until after the stage check
questions.why: Practicing the same drill over and over is blocked practice. It scores well during practice but gives poorer long-term learning, and it tends to fool both the learner and the instructor into thinking the skill is learned. Random practice scores worse during the session but better on a test the next day, which is why the AIH ties well-written SBT to better retention [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]. Her poor first landing is that next-day test. A plateau is progress leveling off over a period of time [[25:77|AIH 3-26]], not a drop after one session of blocked practice.

questions.q: In flight you demonstrate turns around a point while explaining each step. Then you hand her the controls, and she talks herself through her first attempt while you watch. Which step of the telling-and-doing technique did you skip, and what would it have given you?
options: Instructor tells, instructor does; it would have shown her the maneuver once
Learner tells, instructor does; with her explaining while you fly, you could check her understanding and correct a misunderstanding before she is busy flying
Learner tells, learner does; it would have let her think aloud while flying
Evaluation; it would have given her a grade before her first attempt
questions.why: Telling-and-doing adds a transition step between your demonstration and the learner's practice: learner tells, instructor does [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Freed from flying, the learner organizes her thoughts about the steps, you can evaluate her understanding, and a misunderstanding can be corrected before she becomes absorbed in controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. You did give the demonstration, and her talking herself through the attempt was the learner tells, learner does step, so neither was missed.

questions.q: Your classroom lesson on weight and balance has five minutes left. Which close best follows the AIH guidance for the lesson conclusion and the assessment step?
options: Introduce how a CG shift changes stall speed, so learners leave curious about next week
Ask "Does everyone understand?" and dismiss the class when no one objects
Retrace the key points and tie them to the objective, then have each learner work one loading problem to show the objective was met
Skip the review because the material is still fresh, and let the class leave early as a reward
questions.why: An effective conclusion retraces the important elements and relates them to the objective; new ideas should not be introduced there because they are likely to confuse learners [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Before the period ends, the instructor reviews what was covered and asks the learners to demonstrate how well the objectives were met [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. "Does everyone understand?" is a yes/no question that effective quizzing leaves out [[25:142|AIH 6-11]], so silence tells you nothing about whether they can work the problem.

questions.q: You plan a lesson on the heading indicator that starts with the magnetic compass your learner already uses. In the next lesson you leave out Class A, B and C airspace because she flies only in Class D, E and G. Which AIH patterns for developing main points are you using, in that order?
options: Past to present, then known to unknown
Known to unknown, then simple to complex
Simple to complex, then past to present
Past to present, then simple to complex
questions.why: Starting from something the learner already knows, such as the magnetic compass before gyroscopic heading indicators, is the AIH's known-to-unknown example. Leaving out A, B and C airspace for a learner who uses only D, E and G is its simple-to-complex advice to omit less important information at first [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Past to present arranges material in time order and suits topics where history matters, such as tracing radio navigation systems [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Bruner's advice to teach from the known to the unknown makes the same point from learning theory [[25:55|AIH 3-4]].

questions.q: Early in training your learner holds attitude by watching the attitude indicator, makes bank corrections without looking up, and keeps overcorrecting as she chases the needles. What does the AFH say to teach, and what tool may help?
options: Keep about 90 percent of attention outside, check the instruments only briefly, make corrections against the natural horizon, and consider instrument covers for the first hours
Have her fly by instruments only until she stops chasing them, since integrated instruction prepares her for IMC
Split attention evenly between inside and outside so neither reference dominates
Take the instruments out of her scan entirely until after solo, then add them back
questions.why: The integrated method puts about 90 percent of attention on outside references and traffic [[24:66|AFH 3-5]], with no more than about 10 percent inside; corrections are applied with reference to the natural horizon and then rechecked on the instruments. Correcting while still looking inside is the most common beginner error, beginners chase the instruments because of lag and precession, and instrument covers for the first hours can force the learner back outside [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. This training does not prepare a pilot for IMC, and visual and instrument references should stay integrated throughout training [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], so removing the instruments is wrong too.

questions.q: For a presolo lesson on local airspace you wrote a performance-based objective with a description, conditions and criteria. Now you want a test for it. In the AIH's four-step process for choosing an assessment method, which step has that objective already done for you?
options: Determine level-of-learning objectives
List indicators of desired behaviors
Establish criterion objectives
Develop criterion-referenced test items
questions.why: Criterion objectives state the behavior, the conditions and the criteria to be met, and the AIH says that if you developed performance-based objectives for your lesson plans, the criterion objectives have already been formulated [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. Those are the same three elements as a performance-based objective [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. The general level-of-learning objective comes first in the process [[25:139|AIH 6-8]], and the test items come last, written to measure the behaviors in the criterion objective [[25:140|AIH 6-9]].

questions.q: You give your private pilot applicant her last logged training for the practical test on March 10 and endorse her that day. The AIH says the instructor's recommendation is "valid for 60 days." Under 14 CFR 61.39, what is the last day she can take the test on that training without more training and a new endorsement?
options: April 30
May 9
May 31
June 30
questions.why: The endorsement must certify training received and logged within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)]]. If she applies in May, the two preceding calendar months are March and April, so March 10 counts. In June they would be April and May, so it does not. That makes May 31 the last day. May 9 is 60 days after March 10, the AIH's figure [[25:183|AIH 9-13]], but the regulation's calendar-month wording is what governs.

questions.q: In the debrief your learner rates his short-field approaches "Perform" because he never went outside standards. You had to call out his airspeed creeping high twice before he fixed it. How do the AIH rubric and process handle this?
options: Record Perform, because in learner-centered grading the learner's self-assessment decides the grade
Record Explain, because he could not fly the approach without help
Grade it a C so he sees it was only average, and move on to the next lesson
Your view fits Practice, since your coaching corrected the deviations; compare the two ratings in discussion and decide his progress together
questions.why: Perform means the learner does it without instructor help and corrects his own errors quickly; Practice means he plans and executes it while your coaching corrects the deviations you identify [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. After his self-assessment you compare your assessment with his and jointly determine his progress, as Linda did when Brian rated himself Perform and she rated him Practice [[25:137|AIH 6-6]] [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. Explain means he still needs assistance to execute the maneuver, and forcing the rubric into an A to F mold is the trap the AIH warns about [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

questions.q: Your homemade presolo knowledge test has 25 questions, all on the airspace around your home airport. Which characteristic of a good test is weakest, and what must you do after the learner takes it?
options: Comprehensiveness; it should also sample parts 61 and 91 and the airplane's flight characteristics and limits, and you must review every incorrect answer with him before authorizing solo
Discrimination; post the scores so he can compare himself with other learners
Usability; reprint it in larger type, then let him grade his own answers
Objectivity; rewrite it as essay questions, then file it in his training folder
questions.why: Comprehensiveness is how well a test samples the overall objectives, like measuring compression on every cylinder rather than one [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]. The presolo test must address the applicable parts of 61 and 91, the airspace rules and procedures for the solo airport, and the flight characteristics and operational limits of the make and model, and the instructor must give it and review all incorrect answers before authorizing solo [[60:271|14 CFR 61.87(b)]]. Discrimination matters little where minimum standards count far more, and essays are harder, not easier, to grade objectively [[25:136|AIH 6-5]].

questions.q: On a dual cross-country your learner forgets to lean the mixture after leveling off on the first leg, and again on the second. You plan to save every comment for a full debrief the next morning. What does the AIH say?
options: Waiting is best, because a critique should come only after the learner has rested
Say nothing during the flight so he discovers the error himself, since learners always find their own mistakes
Lean the mixture yourself each time without comment to keep the flight on schedule
Tell him as soon after the performance as you can so he does not practice the mistake; a critique belongs right after the performance, while details are easy to recall
questions.why: Learners should be told about their progress as soon after the performance as possible and should not be allowed to practice mistakes, because unlearning a mistake is harder than learning it right the first time. The AIH also notes that in complex skills mistakes are not always apparent to the learner [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]. A critique should come immediately after the performance, while the details are easy to recall [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]. Fixing it silently teaches him nothing, and errors that are not identified will probably be perpetuated through faulty practice [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

questions.q: Two learners make the same flare error. One is timid and easily discouraged; the other works harder after brisk feedback. How does the AIH want you to critique them?
options: Name the error and how to fix it for both, but fit the tone and amount of criticism to each person, since too much criticism discourages a timid learner
Identically, because being consistent means every learner hears the same words for the same error
Skip the correction for the timid learner so she keeps her confidence
Praise the timid learner after every landing to balance out any criticism
questions.why: Too much criticism may discourage a timid person, while brisk instruction may push another learner to work harder [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. A flexible assessment fits its tone, technique and content to the occasion and to the learner [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]. Either way the error has to be identified with how to correct it, or it will be perpetuated through faulty practice, and praise given too freely becomes valueless [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Being consistent means your standards do not change from one day to the next, not that every learner hears identical words [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

questions.q: Your recent experience period is about to end. In the preceding 24 calendar months you endorsed 6 applicants for practical tests. To use the practical test endorsement option of 14 CFR 61.197, how many of them must have passed on the first attempt?
options: At least 3
At least 4
At least 5
All 6
questions.why: That option needs at least 5 applicants endorsed in the preceding 24 calendar months, with at least 80 percent of all those endorsed passing on the first attempt [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(b)(2)(i)]]. 80 percent of 6 is 4.8, so 5 must pass first time; 4 of 6 is only about 67 percent. If you fall short, another option is an approved flight instructor refresher course completed within the preceding 3 calendar months [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(b)(2)(iii)]].

questions.q: You had yesterday off. Since 0700 today you have given 2.5, 2.0 and 1.8 hours of flight training. At 1800 a learner asks for a 1.5-hour flight lesson. What is the best answer?
options: No; the 8-hour limit also counts the time you spent on the ground between flights
Yes; the total stays under 8 hours, and meeting the rule shows the risk is acceptable
The lesson is legal at 7.8 hours in 24 consecutive hours, but the P in PAVE covers you too, so check yourself with IMSAFE before you accept
No; a flight instructor may give no more than 6 hours of flight training in one day
questions.why: In any 24 consecutive hours a flight instructor may not conduct more than 8 hours of flight training [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]]. 2.5 + 2.0 + 1.8 + 1.5 = 7.8 hours, so it is legal. But the P in PAVE applies to the instructor as well as the learner [[25:187|AIH 10-3]], and instructor aeromedical risks should be monitored constantly with IMSAFE [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. A legal total does not by itself make the risk acceptable, and the rule limits flight training, not time on the ground.

questions.q: Your school keeps a training folder with lesson plans and grade sheets for each learner. Which record does 14 CFR 61.189 itself require for each person you endorse for a knowledge test, and for how long?
options: The person's name, the kind of test, the date and the result, kept at least 3 years
A complete training folder with every lesson plan used, kept at least 3 years
The person's name and the date only, kept at least 2 years
A copy of the knowledge test report, kept until the practical test is passed
questions.why: 14 CFR 61.189 requires you to sign the logbook of each person you train and to keep a record of each person you endorse for a knowledge or practical test, showing the kind of test, the date and the results, plus the name and date for each solo endorsement, all kept at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]]. The AIH recommends a training folder with lesson plans and training records, also kept at least 3 years [[25:152|AIH 7-8]], but that is good practice, not the regulation's list.

questions.q: On a dual cross-country your learner describes the hazards of the building cumulus ahead clearly, but only after you ask what concerns her, and then she waits for you to suggest a diversion. Which SRM grade fits today's flight?
options: Explain
Practice
Manage-Decide
Perform
questions.why: Explain means the learner can identify, describe and understand the risks but needs to be prompted to identify risks and make decisions. Practice requires an active decision maker, and Manage-Decide means she gathers the important data, weighs each course of action and decides with no instructor intervention needed [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Perform belongs to the maneuver rubric, not the SRM rubric [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. To move her up, keep handing her real decisions, such as the go/no-go call on the weather before each flight, while the final choice to fly stays with you [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

questions.q: Your learner now recovers from power-off and power-on stalls consistently. What does the AIH say should come next so the training matches how stall/spin accidents really happen?
options: More full stalls at lower altitudes so the recoveries feel realistic
Stalls flown while she handles realistic distractions, such as finding a heading to an airport on a chart, so she learns to divide attention and keep control
No more stall practice, since intentional stall practice causes most stall/spin accidents
Distractions added from the very first stall lesson, before she has learned the recovery
questions.why: NTSB data show most stall/spin accidents happened when the pilot's attention was diverted; intentional stall practice seldom caused an accident, and the real danger was inadvertent stalls induced by distractions in routine flight [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. The most effective training creates distractions while the learner practices certain maneuvers, and you teach her to divide attention while keeping control [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Planned distractions are for tasks already mastered to some degree, which is different from distracting a learner during early skill learning [[25:78|AIH 3-27]], and teaching stalls without enough altitude to recover creates a hazard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

questions.q: During a dual lesson your learner rolls into a steep turn without clearing first. You had already looked and seen no traffic. What does the AIH say to do?
options: Nothing this time, since you had cleared the area and the instructor owns the lookout in dual flight
Note it for the postflight debrief so you do not interrupt the maneuver
Correct it right away; learners who think you do all the scanning never build the habit, and the two of you share the lookout
Take the controls and demonstrate the steep turn again from the beginning
questions.why: Any tendency of a learner to enter maneuvers without first checking for other traffic needs to be corrected immediately, because learners who believe the instructor does all the scanning never develop constant vigilance. Flight instructors were on board in 37 percent of the midair collisions in one study [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. In dual instruction, you and the learner are both responsible for the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Waiting for the debrief lets the habit form, and a new demonstration does not address the missing clearing check.

questions.q: Your learner's first soft-field takeoff is today at a towered airport. Where does the AIH want most of your teaching on airspeeds, pitch attitude and visual references to happen?
options: During the takeoff roll, while she can feel what you are describing
On the climbout, once the airplane is clear of the runway
After the flight only, so nothing distracts her on the first attempt
In the preflight briefing and before you call the tower, so the flight deck stays sterile during the takeoff itself
questions.why: A takeoff takes only seconds, and anything said during it may not be heard or processed; it can also cause a missed tower call. The AIH says to do most of the teaching, such as airspeeds, pitch attitudes, visual references, control inputs and engine parameters, before contacting the tower, which helps keep a sterile flight deck and supports collision avoidance [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. The explanation phase of demonstration-performance happens before the flight lesson in a thorough preflight briefing [[25:175|AIH 9-5]], so saving it all for after the flight leaves her to try the maneuver unprepared.
